description: 1.d4 without committing to the Queen's Gambit. White builds a flexible, classical centre and waits to see Black's setup before choosing between the London System, the Colle, the Catalan, or a c4 push. Most popular first move on Chess.com — solid, low-theory, and well suited to positional players who want to outplay opponents in the middlegame rather than memorise sharp lines.

1.e4 e5 with neither side committing yet — the umbrella for classical open games like the Italian, Ruy Lopez, Scotch, and Petrov. Leads to fast development, central tension, and direct piece play. Ideal for players who want to learn classical principles (control the centre, develop knights before bishops, castle early) without diving into a single sharp system.
1.e4 (umbrella label that hasn't yet committed to a system). Functionally the same as "King's Pawn Game" — see that entry.

1.e4 e6: Black builds a solid pawn chain (e6 + d5) and accepts a slightly cramped position in exchange for a rock-solid structure and a clear pawn-break plan (...c5, sometimes ...f6). White typically gets a space advantage; Black plays for the long game and counterattacks the d4 pawn or White's overextended kingside. Suits patient, defensive players who like manoeuvring and deep strategic battles.

1.e4 d5: Black challenges the centre on move one and accepts an early queen sortie (after 2.exd5 Qxd5) to get a simple, solid game with a clear plan. Easy to learn — a few lines cover most situations — and a great choice for club players who want a system response to 1.e4 without the theory burden of the Sicilian or French.

1.e4 c5: the most ambitious response to 1.e4, played in roughly 25% of master games. Black declines the symmetrical 1...e5 to fight for the centre asymmetrically with ...c5 and (usually) ...d6 / ...e6. The richest theoretical battleground in chess — Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov, Taimanov, Kan, Scheveningen, Classical — and the only mainstream response where Black scores better than White on average. Suits aggressive, tactical players willing to invest in theory for winning chances with the black pieces.

1.e4 c6: Black prepares ...d5 with a pawn move first, getting the same central challenge as the French but without locking in the light-squared bishop. The result is a solid, structurally sound defense with clear plans and far less theory than the Sicilian — the basics can be learned in an evening. Suits positional players who want stability and simplicity, and reliably scores almost as well as the Sicilian for Black.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4: the classical attacking opening — fast development, immediate pressure on f7, and natural plans like d3, c3, and a queenside expansion (the Giuoco Pianissimo) or sharper lines like the Evans Gambit. The friendliest mainline opening for new players, and still played at the very top level by players like Carlsen. Good for anyone who wants a principled, attacking 1.e4 weapon without the theory load of the Ruy Lopez.

1.Nf3 with the idea of fianchettoing the king's bishop and challenging Black's centre from the flank (often transposing to the English or Catalan). Hypermodern in spirit: White invites Black to occupy the centre, then undermines it with c4 and Bg2 pressure on the long diagonal. Suits flexible, strategic players who like a wide range of transpositional options and don't want to be forced into mainline 1.d4 or 1.e4 theory.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4: develops the bishop to its best square immediately and keeps options open between a slow Italian-style buildup or a sharper d4 + Nf3 setup. Often used as a sneaky way to reach a Vienna or a King's Gambit declined while sidestepping Black's preparation against the Italian. Quietly tricky and a favourite of attacking players who want to surprise their opponents on move two.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6: hypermodern — Black lets White build a big pawn centre, then attacks it with ...Bg7, ...c5 or ...e5 breaks. Sharp, double-edged play; both sides are usually castling on opposite wings or racing for the centre. Suits aggressive players who like dynamic, theoretical-but-not-overwhelming openings and don't mind defending a slightly worse position to play for the counterattack.

1.d4 d5 2.c4: White offers a flank pawn to deflect Black's d-pawn and seize the centre. The cornerstone of classical 1.d4 play — leads to the Queen's Gambit Declined (the most respected mainline reply), the Slav, the QGA, and the Semi-Slav. The most theoretical 1.d4 system but rewards strategic understanding more than memorisation. Suits positional players who want a principled, time-tested White repertoire.

1.e4 Nc6: Black challenges the centre with a knight before deciding on a pawn structure. Avoids most of White's prepared 1.e4 theory and steers the game into less-charted positions where understanding beats memorisation. Solid but offbeat — a good choice for players who want to dodge mainline preparation as Black against 1.e4.

1.c4: a flank opening where White stakes a claim on d5 from the side instead of pushing a centre pawn. Hugely flexible — can transpose into Reversed Sicilians, the Catalan, or pure English structures with a fianchettoed king's bishop and Nc3 pressure. Beloved by strategic, manoeuvring players who like rich middlegames over forcing lines.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6: a solid but passive setup that prioritises pawn structure over piece activity. Black accepts a cramped position with the goal of slowly equalising. Less common at high levels because Black's pieces struggle for breathing room, but a reliable workhorse for defensive players who don't want to learn Sicilian theory.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3: combines classical Italian-style development with the threat of an early f4 (the Vienna Gambit) for a surprise attacking game. Less theoretical than the Ruy Lopez and richer than the Italian — a great middle-ground for attacking 1.e4 players who want flexibility between quiet positional play and sharp gambit lines.

1.e4 g6 (or 1.d4 g6): pure hypermodernism — Black fianchettoes the king's bishop on move one and decides on a central plan later. Ultra-flexible: can transpose to the Pirc, the King's Indian, or independent Modern lines. Suits creative, transpositional players who like positions where understanding beats memorisation, and who don't mind giving White a temporary space advantage to counterstrike later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4: White breaks the centre immediately and forces simplifications — straightforward, tactical, and far less theoretical than the Ruy Lopez. Often produces clear-cut middlegames where one side is up a tempo or has the better structure. Suits attacking players who want a principled 1.e4 weapon they can master in a weekend.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5: the gold standard of 1.e4 — White attacks Black's defender of e5 and angles for a long-term grip on the centre. Deep theory across a dozen mainlines (Berlin, Marshall, Closed, Open, Exchange) but rewards the work: White scores ~55% in master games. The deepest, richest classical opening — what serious 1.e4 players graduate to once the Italian feels too placid.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6: Black answers the attack on e5 by counter-attacking e4 instead of defending. Famous for being drawish at the top level — Black aims to equalise quickly and reach symmetrical, balanced middlegames. A reliable, low-risk defense with no need for deep memorisation. Suits patient, accurate players who want to neutralise sharp 1.e4 attackers.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6: the most respected mainline response to the Queen's Gambit. Black holds the centre with a solid pawn chain (e6 + d5), develops naturally, and plays for slow, structural equalisation. Cornerstone of classical Black repertoires — Capablanca, Karpov, Carlsen all leaned on it. Suits patient positional players who want a battle-tested defense against 1.d4 with rich strategic content.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6: Black gives up the centre, fianchettoes the king's bishop, and aims for a kingside pawn storm later (...f5, ...g5, ...f4) while White expands on the queenside. One of the most uncompromising openings in chess — both sides race their attacks on opposite wings. Beloved by attacking players (Fischer, Kasparov, Nakamura) who want maximum winning chances with the black pieces.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6: like the QGD but Black supports d5 with the c-pawn instead of the e-pawn, keeping the light-squared bishop free. Famously solid — the c6 pawn anchors d5 and the bishop can develop actively. Lower theory than the QGD or Semi-Slav and very hard to break down. Suits structural, classical players who want a no-nonsense reply to 1.d4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4: Black pins the c3 knight and threatens to double White's c-pawns — combining classical centre control with hypermodern pressure on the long diagonal. Considered one of the soundest Black defenses against 1.d4 ever invented, played at every level from beginner to world champion. Suits strategic players who like positions where structure and piece coordination decide the game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4: Black grabs the gambit pawn and concedes the centre, planning to return the pawn later in exchange for active piece play and an isolated queen pawn target on d4. More forcing than the QGD and far less theoretical. Suits dynamic players who like to give back a small structural concession for active piece play.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 e6: combines the Slav (...c6) and the QGD (...e6) for the most flexible — and theoretically richest — defense to 1.d4. Lines like the Meran, the Botvinnik, and the Anti-Moscow are some of the sharpest in all of chess. The opening of choice for players who want maximum complexity and winning chances out of an objectively solid defense.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5: pure hypermodernism — Black lets White build a huge pawn centre on d4 + e4 + c4, then dismantles it with ...c5, ...Bg7 pressure on the long diagonal, and tactical pinpricks at every move. One of the most theoretically demanding Black defenses but deadly when prepared. Suits sharp, well-prepared attacking players (Fischer, Kasparov, Svidler).

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3: White fianchettoes the king's bishop on g2 and plays for long-term pressure on the long diagonal and on Black's queenside. Considered one of the most positionally demanding openings in chess — Karpov, Kramnik, and Carlsen all swear by it. Suits patient, positional players who like to squeeze out wins from minimal advantages over 60-move games.

1.d4 f5: Black takes the kingside fight to White from move one, accepting structural weaknesses (a backward e-pawn, weak king) for active piece play and attacking chances. Three main variations (the Leningrad with ...g6, the Stonewall with ...d5/...e6/...c6, the Classical with ...e6) give very different middlegame characters. Suits aggressive players who want to play for the win as Black against 1.d4.

1.e4 Nf6: Black provokes White into pushing pawns (e5, d4, c4, sometimes f4) and then attacks the overextended centre with ...d6, ...c5, and counterstrokes against the d4 pawn. A pure provocation opening — Black welcomes the space disadvantage, banking on White's pawns becoming weaknesses. Suits creative players who like asymmetrical positions and don't mind defending precisely.

1.b3: a flexible flank opening where White fianchettoes the queen's bishop on b2 and steers the game into hypermodern positions. Less theoretical than mainline 1.d4 / 1.e4 systems and very hard for Black to prepare against. Named after Aron Nimzowitsch and Bent Larsen, who used it to reach the world championship candidates. Suits flexible, transpositional players.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5: White pins the f6 knight on move two, threatening to double Black's pawns or trade the bishop for the knight — disrupting Black's normal development. A great anti-Indian weapon that sidesteps the King's Indian, Nimzo, and Grünfeld in one move. Lower theory than mainline 1.d4 systems and a favourite of attacking players who want to dodge prepared Black defenses.

1.Nf3 followed by g3, Bg2, d3, Nbd2, e4 — the King's Indian setup played with White (a tempo up). A pure system opening: White plays the same moves regardless of what Black does, then strikes with e5 or kingside expansion. Easy to learn, hard to refute. Suits players who want a low-theory White system they can apply against any Black setup.

1.d4 followed by Bf4 (and c3, e3, Nf3, Nbd2): a system opening where White plays the same setup regardless of Black's response. Solid, durable, and almost impossible for Black to mess up against — but also rarely produces an opening advantage. Famous as a beginner-friendly weapon that scales all the way to the world championship (Carlsen used it). Suits players who want zero opening prep and a reliable middlegame.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 (and after 3.d5 e6): Black creates an asymmetric pawn structure with the half-open e-file and dynamic queenside play. Sharp and double-edged — Black has long-term weaknesses but counts on active piece play and the ...b5 break. Suits aggressive players who want to fight for the initiative as Black against 1.d4.

1.f4: White stakes a kingside claim immediately, planning a Stonewall-style setup or a Leningrad reversed. Sharp and offbeat — accepts a slightly weakened king for kingside attacking chances. A great surprise weapon at club level; rare at the top because of how committal it is.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 (umbrella for both Accepted and Declined): the most romantic opening in chess history. White sacrifices a pawn to crack open the centre and the f-file. See "King's Gambit Accepted" / "King's Gambit Declined" for the specific branches.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4: the most famous gambit in chess history — White sacrifices a pawn to open the f-file and the centre, banking on initiative and rapid attack. Almost unplayable at modern top level (computers like 2...exf4 too much), but a dazzling tactical tourist trail at club level. Suits romantic, attacking players who want sharp lines and crushing attacks even at the cost of objective soundness.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop to b7 and plays for control of e4 and the long diagonal — a solid, ultra-respectable Black system that complements the Nimzo-Indian (which Black plays when White goes 3.Nc3 instead). Suits structural players who want a solid, theory-light pair of replies to 1.d4 with the Nimzo + QID combo.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+: like the Nimzo, but Black checks before White plays Nc3, reaching slightly different (and lower-theory) middlegames. A pragmatic alternative to the Nimzo for Black players who want similar ideas without learning the deeper Nimzo theory.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5: Black accepts an isolated queen pawn (after dxc5 and ...exd5) for active piece play. Considered one of the most principled (and one of the riskiest) Black defenses against the Queen's Gambit. Suits dynamic players who prefer active pieces over a stronger pawn structure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6: classical symmetrical development before any commitment. Often leads to the Glek (4.g3), the Spanish (4.Bb5), or the Italian (4.Bc4) setups. A clean way to play 1.e4 e5 from either side without diving into Ruy Lopez theory.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6: like the King's Indian but with ...d6 first and a slower, more flexible setup. Black often delays ...g6 and plays a small-centre defense aiming for ...e5. Solid, low-theory alternative to the KID for players who like the structures but not the sharp memorisation.

1.Nf3 with the idea of a slow positional buildup (often with d4 + e3 + b3 / Bb2). Reaches Reversed Slav, Colle, or Catalan structures depending on how Black responds. Practical and flexible — a favourite for transpositional players who want to dodge mainline 1.d4 / 1.e4 theory.

1.d4 Nf6: the umbrella catch-all for any 1.d4 Nf6 line that hasn't yet committed to a system. Almost always transposes into the King's Indian, Nimzo, Bogo, Queen's Indian, Grünfeld, or Old Indian. Listed here for completeness — practically you'll be in one of those families by move 4.

1.g3 — see "King's Fianchetto Opening". This entry collects lines that start 1.g3 and stay independent (rather than transposing to the English or Réti). Solid hypermodern setup with fianchetto pressure on the long diagonal.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 with Black declining to take the f-pawn. Black avoids the sharpest Accepted lines and plays for a normal central battle, often with ...Bc5 or ...d6 setups. A practical anti-Gambit response that doesn't require the heavy theoretical knowledge of accepting.

1.d4 g6 / 1.e4 g6 with an early ...c5 — a hypermodern, highly transpositional Modern/Sicilian hybrid where Black fianchettoes and pushes ...c5 to challenge the centre. Offbeat but theoretically sound; a niche favourite of players who want unfamiliar middlegame structures.

1.e4 e5 2.d4: White breaks the centre on move two, accepting an early queen sortie after 2...exd4 3.Qxd4 in exchange for development pressure. Largely abandoned at master level (the queen on d4 wastes time when Black plays ...Nc6) but a tricky surprise weapon at club level. Suits attacking players who like sharp, forcing lines.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 (with Black not yet playing ...Nf6): a flexible classical setup, often a stepping stone to the Four Knights or the Italian. Low theory but rarely produces an opening edge.

family: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defense
description: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5: a sharp gambit branch of the Vienna where Black hits back in the centre instead of accepting. Tactically rich, theoretically narrow — a great surprise weapon for both colours.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3: White prepares an immediate d4 push to grab the centre. Mostly a sideline at modern top level (Black equalises with 3...d5 or 3...Nf6) but a fun club-level surprise weapon for attacking players.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5: an aggressive, dubious-but-tricky gambit where Black throws the f-pawn to disrupt White's centre. Objectively bad, but produces dazzling tactics if White doesn't know the antidote. Pure surprise weapon territory.
(see Latvian Gambit) — White takes the offered f-pawn; tactical chaos follows.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5: Black sacrifices a pawn for piece activity and an open centre. Refuted at the top level, dangerous at club level — exactly the kind of "I bet they don't know this" weapon some players love.

1.d4 e5: Black sacrifices a pawn on move one to open the position and trick White into a back-rank disaster (the famous Englund mate trap). Unsound against accurate play but hilarious when it works. A tournament-trap weapon, not a serious repertoire choice.

1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 with subtler Black follow-ups (or White declining outright with 2.d5). The non-trap Englund branch — usually transposes into a worse-Black Old Indian or pawn-down position with no compensation.

1.b4 (the Sokolsky/Orangutan): White grabs the queenside immediately and fianchettoes the queen's bishop on b2. Offbeat and rare at master level but has a small following among club players who want to dodge mainline preparation. Unbalanced positions with good practical chances at lower levels.

1.d4 d5 2.e4: White sacrifices a pawn in the centre for rapid development and attacking chances against Black's king. Unsound at top level (Black just keeps the pawn), but a famously dangerous club-level weapon. Suits aggressive 1.d4 players who want chaos.
1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4: see Blackmar-Diemer Gambit. The mainline accepted branch.
1.d4 d5 2.e4 (Black declines): less critical than the accepted lines; usually leads to French- or Caro-style structures where White's gambit was a wasted pawn move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5: Black sacrifices the b-pawn for long-term queenside pressure on the half-open a- and b-files. A famously positional gambit — Black's compensation is structural, not tactical. Suits patient strategic players who like to play down a pawn for the long-term grind.
(see Benko Gambit family)
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 with White declining to take. Avoids the sharp accepted lines but usually concedes Black easy equality. The pragmatic anti-Benko response.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5: White pins the f6 knight early and plays for an aggressive setup against the Queen's Pawn structure. Offbeat at master level but a sharp club-level weapon that sidesteps the heaviest 1.d4 theory.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5: White develops the queen's bishop actively before committing to a system. Solid, low-theory, and a favourite of players who want a flexible 1.d4 weapon that avoids the King's Indian and Grünfeld jungles.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3: White builds a pyramid (d4 + e3 + c3) and aims for the kingside attack with a later e4 break. A pure system opening — White plays the same setup every game. Easy to learn, decent results at club level, lacks bite at master level.
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 (Akiba Rubinstein's pet system) — leads to similar structures as the Colle and the QGD Exchange. Solid, low-theory, suited to positional players.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 (with an early Bf4): a tricky modern London-system cousin played by Rapport and Jobava. Avoids mainline 1.d4 theory and aims for unbalanced middlegames. Surprisingly hard to prepare against.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5: a Grünfeld where White fianchettoes and avoids the sharpest mainlines. Lower theory than the regular Grünfeld and a pragmatic alternative for both colours.
A QID branch where White plays a quieter setup with e3 instead of the mainline g3 / Bg2. Less ambitious and rarely seen at top level.

family: Queen's Indian Defense, with e3, Bb4+ Line
description: A specific QID-with-e3 sub-variation where Black checks early. Highly transpositional sideline.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 (with no early ...g6): a Pirc/Philidor hybrid where Black plays a small-centre setup and aims for ...e5 break. Solid, offbeat, and a useful surprise weapon against 1.e4.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 c6 — a solid, ultra-passive defense with similarities to the Caro-Kann and Pirc. Low theory, low ambition; a fortress system for defensive players.

1.e4 b6: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop on move one and builds a hypermodern setup. Offbeat but solid; a great surprise weapon at club level for players who like the Modern Defense's structures but want to dodge mainline anti-Modern theory.
1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop and aims for ...Bb4+ or ...f5 setups. Highly unbalanced and a favourite of attacking players who want to dodge mainline 1.d4 prep.
1.e4 a6: an extreme hypermodern joke-with-teeth — Black plays ...a6 first to prepare ...b5 and a queenside fianchetto. Famously beat Karpov in one game. Mostly a club-level curiosity.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6: an offbeat way to provoke d5 and reach unusual King's-Indian-style structures. Rarely seen at top level.
A 1.d4 Nc6 line aiming for ...e5. Offbeat; usually transposes to a Chigorin-flavoured QGD or a worse-Black centre.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nf6: an unusual move-order combining Slav and Indian themes. Mostly a transpositional curiosity.
A 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b6 line that mimics QID without the c4 push. Offbeat sideline.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 with an early ...Bb7 + ...Be7. Sub-variation of the QID family that's mostly a positional-curiosity sideline.
A 1.d4 d5 system named after Artur Yusupov and Akiba Rubinstein — a positional Colle/Rubinstein hybrid favoured by patient players.
A King's-Indian-flavoured 1.d4 Nf6 line where Black delays ...g6. Offbeat sub-family.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6 (skipping ...e6): an unusual move-order trick to reach QID-style positions. Sideline.
1.Nh3: an offbeat, semi-joke opening where the knight goes to the rim. Borderline unsound; mostly seen in blitz pranks.
1.d4 d5 2.Qd3: a joke / shock opening that develops the queen far too early. Rare and unsound.
1.e3 e5 2.c4: a slow, hypermodern setup where White postpones d4 and plays for an English-like structure with reversed colours. Very rare.
1.a3: a tempo-wasting opening that plans to reverse colours into a Black system. Too passive to be taken seriously.
An obscure 1.d4 sideline. Mostly a curiosity.
1.e4 f6: weakens Black's king from move one and develops nothing. Not a real defense.
1.f3: among the worst first moves in chess — weakens the king and develops nothing. Joke / handicap territory only.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nf3 b5: a sharp pawn-sacrifice gambit. Tactical surprise weapon, mostly seen at club level.
(see Blumenfeld Countergambit) — the accepted branch of the Blumenfeld Countergambit family.
1.e4 e5 2.Ke2: the famous joke opening popularised by Hikaru Nakamura. Loses castling rights immediately. Pure entertainment, not real chess.
1.e4 g5: an outlandish kingside flank attack that weakens Black's king for nothing. "Borg" is "Grob" backwards — and this is the Black version of an already-bad opening.
1.d4 f5 2.e4: a semi-joke gambit against the Dutch. Unsound but tricky.
1.e4 h6: a joke / shock defense weakening the kingside. Not real theory.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 — see Center Game; the accepted branch.
1.h3: a tempo-wasting flank pawn move. Joke territory.
An offbeat 1.h3 + 1.a3 setup. Not serious chess.
1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3: White sacrifices one or two pawns for a roaring development lead and attacking chances. Unsound at top level but a thrilling club-level surprise.
(see Danish Gambit) — Black takes the offered pawns; sharp tactical territory.
(see Danish Gambit) — Black declines the gambit and plays a normal classical game.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4: an early ...Ne4 sortie. Offbeat sideline.
An obscure White system. Rarely seen.
1.e4 f5: a kingside Black gambit that mostly loses material. Surprise weapon only.
A 1.c4 + b4 hybrid setup mixing English and Polish themes. Niche surprise weapon.
A catch-all label for highly transpositional system openings. Not a real "opening" by itself.
1.e4 f6 2.d4 Kf7: extreme joke territory — Black walks the king out for no reason.
An obscure White system. Rarely seen.
1.e4 h5: weakens the kingside. Joke defense.
1.g4: the most famous "bad" opening — weakens White's king and pieces. Has cult fans who play it for chaos but it's objectively poor.
An obscure Black sideline.
A passive double-fianchetto setup where Black retreats every minor piece to the second rank and waits for White to overextend. Rarely played seriously.
1.d4 e6: an offbeat move-order to a French / Queen's Indian / Dutch hybrid. Sideline.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5: White sacrifices a knight for an attack. Unsound; club-level prank only.
1.h4: extreme flank pawn — borderline joke.
1.d4 e6 2.c4 Bb4+: an early bishop check. Sideline of the English Defense / Bogo-Indian family.
A specific KIA branch where Black plays an early ...Bf5. Sideline.
A specific KIA branch where Black plays an early ...e6. Sideline.
The umbrella for 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 lines that haven't yet committed. Practical use is to flag move orders, not as a "system".
A whimsical 1.b4 sideline with no serious theory.
An ironically named flank-pawn defense. Joke territory.
The mainline London bishop development (Bd3). Solid, system-style.
A passive London variation where the bishop goes to e2 instead of d3. Very quiet.
1.d3 — a low-ambition system opening that plans to reverse-Philidor or transpose. Rare.
An obscure 1.d4 sideline.
1.d4 with an early Nf3 + Nbd2 setup. Joke-ish nickname for a passive system.
1.d4 b5: Black's queenside flank gambit. Offbeat surprise weapon.
A 1.b4 sideline where Black plays ...d5. Niche.
1.e4 e5 2.Bb5: White plays a Spanish-style bishop development immediately, before Nf3. Tricky offbeat weapon.
A specific 1.d4 sideline. Niche.
Sub-variation of the Rapport-Jobava family. See parent entry.
1.e4 d6 with no follow-up commitment — usually a Pirc/Modern shell-game. Offbeat label more than a real system.
An older name for the Modern Defense (1...g6). Listed as a separate family in some databases for historical reasons.
1.c3: a hypermodern, ultra-passive opening that plans to reverse-Caro-Kann. Rare.
A move-order curiosity in the Semi-Slav family.
1.Na3: a joke knight-on-rim opening. Borderline unplayable.
An obscure 1.e4 system. Rare.
1.Nc3: a flexible knight move that often transposes to the Van Geet (Dunst) Sicilian or unusual French-flavoured positions. Niche.
1.e3: a passive, ultra-flexible opening. Rare at any serious level.
A specific Benoni-flavoured sideline. Very rare.
1.d4 d6 2.Nf3 Bg4: an offbeat early bishop development against 1.d4. Niche.
1.e4 a5: weakens the queenside for nothing. Joke territory.
1.a4: a tempo-wasting flank move. Joke territory.
An obscure 1.d4 sideline. Niche.
An obscure 1.d4 sideline named for Johannes Zukertort. Rare.
